stem: Which layer of the TCP/IP stack is responsible for adding the IP addresses of the sender and the receiver?

options.rationale: Correct: the internet layer makes packets with IP addresses.
The application layer produces the data and follows rules such as HTTP.
The transport layer adds port numbers.
The link layer adds MAC addresses.

explanation: Packets carry IP addresses, so this is the internet layer.

stem: What does the transport layer of the TCP/IP stack add to the data?

options.content: Port numbers and a sequence number
options.rationale: Correct: these form the segment header.

options.content: The IP addresses of the sender and receiver
options.rationale: These are added by the internet layer.

options.content: The MAC addresses of the two ends of the link
options.rationale: These are added by the link layer.
Keys are not a transport header.

explanation: Segments carry port numbers and sequence numbers.

stem: What is the name of the unit of data created at the link layer?

options.rationale: A segment is made at the transport layer.
Correct.
A packet is made at the internet layer.
A message is data at the application layer.

explanation: Data, segment, packet, frame.

stem: Why are network protocols arranged in layers?

options.content: It makes all networks use the same cable
options.rationale: Layers do not decide the cable.

options.content: It makes the data travel faster along the cables and wires of the whole network
options.rationale: Layers organise the work; they do not speed up signals.

options.content: It removes the need for addresses
options.rationale: Addresses are still needed in the layers.

options.content: Each layer does one job and can be changed without affecting the others
options.rationale: Correct.

explanation: Layering simplifies design and allows layers to be replaced.

stem: A router forwards a packet to the next network. Up to which TCP/IP layer does the router need to process the packet?

options.rationale: A router does not need to read the application data.
A router does not need the port numbers to route a packet.
Correct: it reads the destination IP address.
It must at least read the IP address to forward the packet.

explanation: A router unpacks a frame as far as the packet and uses the IP address.
hints: Which header holds the destination IP address?

stem: Which describes the main difference between TCP and UDP?

options.content: UDP is used at the link layer and TCP is used at the application layer
options.rationale: Both are transport layer protocols.

options.content: TCP uses IP addresses and UDP uses MAC addresses
options.rationale: Both use ports; addresses are handled by lower layers.

options.content: TCP checks that data arrives complete and in order; UDP does not
options.rationale: Correct.
UDP does not resend lost data.

explanation: TCP is reliable and ordered; UDP is faster and leaves recovery to the application.

stem: In the OSI model, which layer formats the data, for example by converting character codes or encrypting it?

options.rationale: The session layer manages the conversation.
The network layer routes packets.
The data link layer makes frames.
Correct: layer 6.

explanation: The presentation layer handles formats, compression and encryption.
hints: Which layer sits between application and session?

stem: A website's pages load, but the browser reports that one image failed and the connection was reset. A technician finds that the fault is that segments are not being numbered and re-ordered. Which layer is most likely at fault?

options.rationale: The link layer sends frames on a single link.
Correct: sequencing and error recovery are done by TCP at the transport layer.
The internet layer routes packets but does not number segments.
The application layer sets the rules for web requests, not the numbering of segments.

explanation: Segment numbering and re-ordering belong to the transport layer.

stem: Each layer of the stack adds its own header to the data it receives from the layer above.
explanation: True. This is encapsulation.

stem: A port number identifies a computer on the internet.
explanation: False. A port number identifies a program or service on the host; the IP address identifies the host.

stem: Match each TCP/IP layer to what it handles.

right.content: IP addresses and routing of packets
MAC addresses, frames and the physical medium
Rules for a service such as HTTP or SMTP
Port numbers, segments and reliable delivery

explanation: Each layer deals with one kind of address or unit.

stem: Match each OSI layer to its function.

right.content: Frames and MAC addresses on one link
Sends the bits as signals over the medium
Formats the data, including compression and encryption
Starts, manages and ends a conversation between programs

explanation: Layers 5, 3, 2, 1 and 6 of the OSI model.
hints: Number the layers from 7 down to 1.

stem: Complete the names of the units of data as a message goes down the TCP/IP stack.

payload.template: The transport layer makes a {{blank:a}}, the internet layer makes a {{blank:b}} and the link layer makes a {{blank:c}}.

explanation: Segment, packet, frame.

stem: Complete the mapping of the OSI model to the TCP/IP model.

payload.template: OSI layers 5, 6 and 7 map to the TCP/IP {{blank:a}} layer. OSI layer 3 maps to the {{blank:b}} layer. OSI layers 1 and 2 map to the {{blank:c}} layer.

explanation: 5-7 application; 3 internet; 1-2 link.

stem: A TCP header is 20 bytes, an IP header is 20 bytes and an Ethernet frame adds 14 bytes of header and 4 bytes of trailer. How many bytes are added to each segment's data to make a frame?
explanation: 58 bytes are added to each piece of data.
hints: Add the TCP header, the IP header and the Ethernet header and trailer.

stem:
The message of 2500 bytes is sent in three frames, as shown.

| Segment | Data (bytes) | Frame (bytes) |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| 1 | 1000 | 1058 |
| 2 | 1000 | 1058 |
| 3 | 500 | 558 |

Headers per frame are 58 bytes. Calculate the total number of bytes sent over the link.
explanation: Total bytes sent = 2500 + 3 × 58 = 2674.

stem: Describe the purpose of the transport layer and the internet layer in the TCP/IP stack. [4]

points.description: The transport layer delivers data between the correct programs on the two hosts using port numbers
It splits data into numbered segments (TCP also checks that all arrive and in order)
The internet layer adds the source and destination IP addresses to make packets
It routes the packets across networks to the destination

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The transport layer splits data into numbered segments and delivers them to the correct program using port numbers; TCP also checks that all arrive and in order. The internet layer adds the source and destination IP addresses to make packets and routes them across networks.

explanation: Ports and segments; addresses and routing.
hints: Name each layer and its job.

stem: Give three advantages of using a layered protocol stack. [3]

points.description: Each layer has one job, so it is easier to design and test
A layer can be changed or replaced without affecting the other layers
Hardware and software from different makers work together because the interfaces are standard

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Each layer has one job, which makes it easier to design and test. A layer can be replaced without changing the others, and equipment from different makers works together because the interfaces are standard.

explanation: Simplicity, replaceability, compatibility.
hints: Mention reuse of one layer by another.

stem: Describe what happens to a message as it is sent from one host to another using the TCP/IP stack. [4]

points.description: At the sender, each layer adds its own header as the message passes down (encapsulation)
The message becomes segments, then packets with IP addresses, then frames with MAC addresses
Routers on the way read the destination IP address and forward the packet
At the receiver, each layer removes its header as the message passes up to the application

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: At the sender each layer adds a header as the message passes down: segments, then packets with IP addresses, then frames with MAC addresses. Routers read the destination IP address and forward the packets. At the receiver each layer removes its header as the message passes up to the application.

explanation: Encapsulation, forwarding, decapsulation.
hints: Describe the sender, the network and the receiver.

stem: Compare the OSI model with the TCP/IP model. [3]

points.description: OSI has seven layers whereas TCP/IP has four
OSI is a reference model for describing networks, but TCP/IP is the set of protocols that the internet actually uses
OSI splits application services into application, presentation and session layers; TCP/IP has a single application layer

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: OSI has seven layers and TCP/IP has four. OSI is a reference model but TCP/IP is the set of protocols that the internet uses. OSI splits application services into three layers, where TCP/IP has one.

explanation: Layers, purpose, application layer.
hints: Compare number of layers, origin and use.

stem: Chipo in Bulawayo sends a request to a web server in Harare over the internet. The browser uses the TCP/IP stack.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which layer produces the HTTP request?

options.rationale: The transport layer splits and numbers the data.
Correct.
The internet layer adds IP addresses.
The link layer creates frames.

parts.explanation: HTTP is an application layer protocol.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which layer adds the port number 443?

options.rationale: The internet layer adds IP addresses.
The link layer adds MAC addresses.
Correct.
The application layer produces the request.

parts.explanation: Port numbers are in the segment header.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State what the internet layer adds to the segment and why.

points.description: The source and destination IP addresses
So that routers can send the packet to the correct network and host

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: It adds the source and destination IP addresses so that routers can send the packet to the correct network and host.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why the MAC address in the frame changes at each router while the IP address stays the same.

points.description: The MAC address identifies the devices at the two ends of one link only
The IP address identifies the final destination, so it stays the same across all the links

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A MAC address only identifies the devices at the two ends of one link, so a new frame is made for each link. The IP address identifies the final destination, so it stays the same.

explanation: Application (HTTP request), transport (port and segments), internet (IP addresses), link (MAC addresses, frame).
hints: Think of the header each layer adds.

stem: A school in Gweru uses a secure web page to submit exam entries. The data is encrypted, sent in packets and carried over a copper cable.

payload.template: The encryption of the data is done by the {{blank:a}} layer. The routing of packets using IP addresses is done by the {{blank:b}} layer. The signals on the copper cable are sent by the {{blank:c}} layer.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: State the number of the OSI layer that makes frames with MAC addresses.
parts.explanation: The data link layer is layer 2.
parts.workedSolution:
1. Frames and MAC addresses belong to the data link layer.
2. The data link layer is layer 2.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State which TCP/IP layer includes the OSI session layer and which TCP/IP layer includes the OSI data link layer.

points.description: Session layer: the application layer
Data link layer: the link layer

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The OSI session layer is part of the TCP/IP application layer and the data link layer is part of the TCP/IP link layer.

explanation: Application 7, presentation 6, session 5; network 3; data link 2; physical 1.
